case_study_insert.main_stem: Ironpine Craft Brewery (ICB) is a private limited company in the craft brewing sector, employing a workforce of 52. Founded in 2014 by Dan Whitmore and Elena Ruiz, it brews hop-forward ales sold to bars, bottle shops and supermarket chains nationwide, using a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership that prizes brewer creativity. ICB plans to invest $540,000 in a canning line to launch a low-alcohol craft lager, financed by a $150,000 bank overdraft and $390,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a unit and a selling price of $16.00, and currently produces 72,000 units a year. ICB faces a defect rate of 3.2% on test cans and a widening skills gap among canning-line operators.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Brewing Quality Report — October 2026: Trial runs of the new canning line produced 18,400 units last quarter at a defect rate of 3.2%, down from 5.6% a year ago. Customer quality complaints fell from 24 to 12 per month. A survey of 500 customers across 30 bars found 61% would buy a low-alcohol craft lager and 49% prefer cans over bottles. Average delivery time to distributors is 2.8 days. Taste-panel testing costs $1,100 per recipe iteration, and 14 of 52 staff have completed advanced brewing certification, while on-the-job coaching on the canning line continues.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Ironpine Craft Brewery as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, increasing costs for businesses using overdrafts. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $12.30 to $12.98 per hour from April 2026, increasing wage bills. (3) Barley, hops and aluminium can input costs have risen 13.2% year-on-year, brewing input inflation is running at 9.8%, while consumer spending on premium craft beer grew 5.1% in the same period.

questions.question_text: ICB plans to fund part of its canning-line investment with a bank overdraft. Explain two advantages for ICB of using retained profit to fund the launch instead of the overdraft.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit costs ICB nothing in interest, which matters because the overdraft is variable-rate and the base interest rate has already risen from 4.25% to 5.0%. Avoiding interest protects the $4.00 contribution per unit on 72,000 units a year and keeps financing costs down while the brewery still carries fixed costs of $180,000 a year — critical for a small craft producer competing with larger beverage groups.

Point 2: Retained profit is permanent capital with no repayment deadline, unlike an overdraft which the bank can demand back at short notice and which is typically reviewed annually. Using the $390,000 retained profit means the $540,000 canning line cannot be snatched away mid-launch, keeps ICB's independence and brewer creativity under the laissez-faire flat structure, and avoids signal risk to supermarket chains that the brewery might be financially stretched during the low-alcohol lager rollout. With 61% of surveyed drinkers interested in the new lager, protecting the launch from financing shocks is worth more to ICB than the modest interest saving an overdraft would offer.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual analysis linked to ICB's launch, overdraft risk and costs.

questions.question_text: ICB is launching its low-alcohol craft lager. Consider social media advertising, sponsorship of craft-beer festivals, or in-store supermarket displays. Which should ICB choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Social media advertising: Targeted ads and short videos can reach the 61% of surveyed customers across 30 bars who said they would buy a low-alcohol craft lager, with precise audience targeting, measurable click-through to the distributor or online ordering, and relatively low cost. Social content fits the craft-beer community's habit of sharing new releases. Weaknesses are ad-blindness, dependence on platform algorithms and the risk that negative comments spread as fast as positive ones.

Sponsorship of craft-beer festivals: Festivals put ICB directly in front of engaged craft drinkers, generate immediate trial, collect feedback and boost authenticity — ideal for a founder-led brand like Ironpine. The cost is moderate and the PR value high, but reach is limited to festival attendees on specific dates, which cannot alone create the national distribution needed across bars, bottle shops and supermarket chains, and results are hard to measure.

In-store supermarket displays: Eye-catching point-of-sale displays would reach supermarket shoppers at the moment of decision in the exact channel where ICB wants listings, support volume orders with chains nationwide, and capture the 49% who prefer cans over bottles through high-visibility can stacks and shelf talkers. Displays depend on retailer cooperation, can be cluttered next to big-brand lager, and offer limited brand storytelling compared with digital or live events.

Recommendation: ICB should choose social media advertising to drive awareness and trial for the launch, supported by in-store supermarket displays once listings land. It delivers the widest, most measurable reach per dollar for a national launch, directly targets the 61% interested in a low-alcohol lager and the 49% preferring cans, and suits a $540,000 rollout with a $150,000 overdraft. Festival sponsorship is rejected as the primary channel because its reach is too limited and too seasonal to carry a national launch alone, and supermarket displays alone are rejected because they reach only existing store footfall without building the brand desire that drives shoppers to seek the product; a full national television campaign would be unaffordable at this scale.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of ICB with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of ICB with a well-justified recommendation explaining why festival sponsorship and supermarket displays alone are rejected as primary channels.

questions.question_text: ICB's flat structure gives brewers laissez-faire freedom, yet the defect rate is 3.2%. Explain two benefits for ICB of introducing quality circles in the brewery.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Quality circles give the 52 staff a regular forum to identify and solve the causes of the 3.2% defect rate, such as can-seaming faults, temperature excursions and contamination points. Because frontline brewers and canning operators know the machinery best, their suggestions target real causes rather than symptoms, reducing waste, rework and rejected consignments while fitting the laissez-faire flat culture that attracted ICB's creative brewers in the first place.

Point 2: Quality circles raise engagement and make staff feel their expertise matters, which strengthens motivation and retention in a specialist skills market. Members who help cut defects from 5.6% toward the 3.2% level build pride and accountability, protecting output of 72,000 units a year and supporting the case for the low-alcohol craft lager launch, since fewer defects mean more sellable product from every batch of the new canning line. In combination, the two benefits cut waste and keep the specialist skills that a laissez-faire craft brewery cannot afford to lose while the launch scales up.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual analysis linked to ICB's defects, skills and launch.

questions.question_text: ICB must tackle the 3.2% defect rate on the canning line. Consider quality control through final-can inspection or quality assurance through preventing defects during brewing. Which should ICB choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Quality control (final-can inspection): Inspecting finished cans catches faults before they reach distributors, directly protecting the 2.8-day delivery promise and the 12 complaints per month now reaching customers. It is fast to introduce, requires only checklist sampling and seam testers, and suits the flat structure because line staff already do visual checks. However, it only detects defects after wasted labour, ingredients and aluminium have been spent, and a sample-based regime can miss intermittent seam failures that a full-process approach would prevent.

Quality assurance (prevention during brewing and canning): QA builds quality into recipes, water treatment, temperature logs, seam settings and operator training so defects never occur, aligning with 14 of 52 staff already holding advanced certification and with the taste-panel programme at $1,100 per iteration. It costs more upfront in training, documentation and process audits, and discipline is harder to sustain under laissez-faire leadership, but it reduces waste at source and supports the new lager's reputation from its first case.

Decision: ICB should choose quality assurance as the primary approach, keeping quality control inspection as a final safety net. Prevention is cheaper per unit saved, addresses root causes of the 3.2% defect rate, and protects the launch of the low-alcohol craft lager where an early quality failure would be more damaging than any cost saving. Quality control alone is rejected as too late and too wasteful, catching faults only after value has been added; the two approaches together give ICB the lowest total cost and the strongest customer trust, with inspection retained as an audit layer for the first six months of the canning line.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of quality control and quality assurance with limited application to ICB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both approaches in the context of ICB.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both approaches in the context of ICB with a well-justified decision covering cost, waste and launch risk.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how ICB's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $180,000 ÷ ($16.00 − $12.00) = $180,000 ÷ $4.00 = 45,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 45,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $16.00 − $12.00 = $4.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $4.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways ICB's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. ICB's managers can compare the 45,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 72,000 units to confirm the brewery is comfortably profitable, with a margin of safety of 27,000 units, informing whether the canning line can carry the low-alcohol lager launch at planned volumes.
2. Contribution per unit of $4.00 lets managers model discounts, for example a 5% price cut to $15.20 would drop contribution to $3.20, letting them judge whether extra volume from a national supermarket listing would still cover the $180,000 fixed costs and the $150,000 overdraft.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $180,000 helps managers set the volume targets used to check the canning line can service a $150,000 overdraft at the higher 5.0% base interest rate and decide when to convert part of the overdraft into a fixed bank loan.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($180,000 ÷ 72,000 units + $12.00 = $14.50 a unit) to benchmark performance across batches, identify waste driving the 3.2% defect rate, and decide whether to renegotiate the $12.00 variable cost with barley, hops and aluminium can suppliers amid the 13.2% input-cost inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 45,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $4.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained in detail: First, ICB's managers can compare the 45,000-unit break-even output with the current 72,000-unit run, confirming a margin of safety of 27,000 units before the canning line ramps up for the low-alcohol craft lager launch. Second, the $4.00 contribution per unit lets managers model discounts requested by supermarket chains — a 5% price cut to $15.20 leaves just $3.20 per unit, so any national listing must still cover the $180,000 fixed costs and the $150,000 overdraft. Third, knowing fixed costs of $180,000 and contribution per unit supports checks on whether the canning line can service the $150,000 overdraft at the higher 5.0% base interest rate, and when part of the overdraft should be converted to a fixed-rate bank loan. Fourth, unit-cost benchmarking ($180,000 ÷ 72,000 units + $12.00 = $14.50 a unit) gives a batch-by-batch yardstick to expose the losses behind the 3.2% defect rate and to challenge barley, hops and aluminium can suppliers amid the 13.2% input-cost inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate ICB's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has ICB's financial position improved? Which of the two ratios gives the stronger evidence, and why? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.42 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.48 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.63 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.67 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $150,000 inventories + $95,000 trade receivables + $25,000 cash = $270,000; 2025 current assets = $185,000 + $120,000 + $35,000 = $340,000. CR 2024 = $270,000 ÷ $190,000 current liabilities = 1.42; CR 2025 = $340,000 ÷ $230,000 = 1.48. AT 2024 = ($270,000 − $150,000) ÷ $190,000 = $120,000 ÷ $190,000 = 0.63; AT 2025 = ($340,000 − $185,000) ÷ $230,000 = $155,000 ÷ $230,000 = 0.67.

Evaluation: Liquidity has modestly improved. Current assets rose from $270,000 to $340,000, and although current liabilities rose from $190,000 to $230,000, short-term coverage still edged up from 1.42 to 1.48. The AT line, which excludes inventories, improved from 0.63 to 0.67, so ICB relies a little less heavily on selling beer stock to pay immediate debts. However, inventories climbed from $150,000 to $185,000 — raw materials for the new lager and finished cans awaiting sale — and trade receivables rose from $95,000 to $120,000, tying up cash. Cash remains thin at just $35,000, leaving little buffer if the overdraft is called in or the 5.0% base rate persists. ICB is funding growth by stretching suppliers and bankers rather than building a cash war chest. Which ratio gives the stronger evidence? The acid test is the stronger indicator of ICB's short-term solvency because it excludes inventories — here stock actually rose from $150,000 to $185,000, so measuring liquidity with stock would have flattered the position — and it improved from 0.63 to 0.67, confirming that the stronger position rests on cash and receivables coverage rather than on piles of beer stock.

Conclusion: ICB's financial position has improved, but only modestly. Both the CR (1.42 to 1.48) and the AT (0.63 to 0.67) moved in the right direction, and the improvement does not depend on inventory. The thin $35,000 cash balance and rising receivables are concerns, so ICB should tighten credit control with bars and distributors, hold inventories lean, and avoid leaning harder on the overdraft while the $540,000 canning line beds in.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables, cash and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether ICB's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for ICB of switching the new lager from glass bottles to aluminium cans.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The 49% of surveyed customers who prefer cans over bottles would be directly reached, and cans suit the pre-chilled, portability-focused low-alcohol lager positioning. Cans are lighter than bottles, cutting freight costs on the 2.8-day delivery routes, they eliminate light-strike flavour faults, stack better in supermarket displays, and appeal to outdoor festival settings where ICB also sponsors — reinforcing the $540,000 canning line business case and the 61% interest in the new lager.

Disadvantage: Switching to aluminium raises exposure to the 13.2% year-on-year rise in can input costs, which would add to the $12.00 variable cost per unit and squeeze the $4.00 contribution per unit unless prices rise or suppliers are renegotiated. The canning line itself demands precise seam control, and 14 of 52 staff still lack advanced certification, so a poorly run transition risks more mis-seams, higher defect rates beyond the current 3.2%, and costly recalls — damaging the new lager's reputation in its launch window.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to ICB's segment, costs and quality.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.0%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 13.2% rise in barley, hops and aluminium can costs will affect ICB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.0%): A 0.75% rise on a $150,000 overdraft adds about $1,125 a year of interest, and on any variable-rate element of future borrowing the cost also rises. The bigger risk is strategic: persistent high rates make the bank review the overdraft limit more critically, and higher rates can dampen consumer spending on premium craft beer beyond the current 5.1% growth. The direct cash impact on ICB is minimal and manageable by fixing borrowing.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $12.98 per hour): The insert gives a 5.5% rise from $12.30 to $12.98 — a derived delta of $0.68 per hour ($12.98 − $12.30; check: 5.5% × $12.30 ≈ $0.68). Production and packing roles anchored to the floor become more expensive from April 2026, and bands above the floor typically shift as well. The insert does not state hours worked, so the annual cash impact cannot be computed precisely; however, for a 52-strong workforce the effect is material and must be offset by the canning line's labour productivity if the 3.2% defect rate falls and rework reduces overtime.

Input cost inflation (13.2% barley, hops and aluminium): These inputs dominate the $12.00 variable cost. Taking the entire variable cost as an explicit upper bound: 13.2% × $12.00 = about $1.58 per unit; at 72,000 units a year that is roughly $113,800 a year (72,000 × $1.58, derivation shown; an upper bound since not all of the $12.00 is barley, hops and aluminium cans). Even a fraction of that bound would directly erode the $4.00 contribution per unit and the margin that must cover fixed costs of $180,000 and service the overdraft. Unlike wages, this cost hits every single unit produced and cannot be absorbed without either raising the $16.00 price or cutting other costs.

Conclusion: The 13.2% input-cost inflation will have the greatest impact. It is bounded at roughly $113,800 a year even if every variable-cost dollar rose with these inputs (an upper bound; the true figure is lower but still clearly above the $1,125 interest impact and, being a percentage applied to the $12.00 variable cost, larger than the derived $0.68-an-hour floor rise in practice), attacks the variable cost on every unit, and cannot be hedged as easily as an overdraft rate. ICB should therefore lock in supply contracts for barley, hops and cans, review the $16.00 price for the new lager, and protect contribution margin, while the wage rise and overdraft cost remain secondary and should be monitored but not allowed to distract from input-cost control.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to ICB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on ICB's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of ICB with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
